chapters.title: A cap, a screen, and thousands of pictures.
Predict one vision model, then search or generate.
Every vision model sees a different picture.
One world, many ways of seeing it.
A new state of the art on EEG and MEG.
Is this mind reading? Does it work on anyone?
A new interface between mind and machine.

cues.text: Can a computer see what you see?
Not read your thoughts.
Just the picture in front of your eyes.
For decades, that took surgery, and electrodes inside the brain.
BHA does it from the outside: a cap of electrodes, and a few hundred milliseconds of brain activity.
Here is the setup.
A volunteer wears a sixty-three electrode E E G cap and watches thousands of photographs, each for a fraction of a second.
We record the brain's response to every picture.
The data is public, the THINGS E E G and M E G benchmarks, so anyone can check our numbers.
Modern decoders don't predict pixels directly.
They predict what a pretrained vision model, usually CLIP, would compute for the image.
Then they search a gallery, or drive an image generator, with that prediction.
It works, and it is where the field was before us.
But it quietly bakes in a choice: which vision model to imitate.
That choice matters.
CLIP cares about meaning.
Self-supervised models like DINO care about shape and parts.
Masked autoencoders care about texture and layout.
Each one sees a picture differently, and the brain predicts some of those views better than others.
Pick one, and you throw the rest away.
Average them into a single target, and you blur their differences.
Here is the idea underneath BHA.
Brains and vision models are looking at the same physical world, and the better they get, the more their representations converge toward it: the platonic representation hypothesis.
We take it one step further.
There is one world, objective and invariant.
And there are many ways of seeing it: CLIP's, DINO's, MAE's, and your brain's, each partial and subjective.
So a decoder should not imitate one view.
It should learn from all of them, because together they describe the world the brain is also looking at.
BHA, Beyond Hierarchical Alignment, stops choosing.
One brain model is trained by four vision teachers at once.
Then, with the brain model frozen, each teacher gets its own small read-out, and learned weights decide how much each teacher's opinion counts.
The image generator is never retrained.
The brain's prediction simply steers it.
Does it work?
Show the model two hundred candidate pictures, and ask which one the person is looking at.
On E E G, BHA picks the right one ninety-three point nine percent of the time.
The previous best was eighty-two point six.
On M E G, sixty-eight point one percent, against forty-eight.
And the gain holds even when we train on only a quarter of the data.
Beyond picking from a gallery, BHA generates.
Every image on the bottom row was produced from one person's E E G response to a photo they had never seen before.
Pixel-level fidelity is up forty-two percent over the strongest published method, and the meaning of the picture comes through more often, with the generator itself left completely untouched.
Two questions we always get.
Is this mind reading?
No.
It decodes the visual response to a picture on a screen, in a lab, with the person's consent.
Does it work on a new person, without training?
Not yet.
Cross-subject accuracy is about thirty percent.
That is sixty times chance, but far below within-subject.
It is the next problem we are solving.
Non-invasive.
Data-efficient.
Built on a generator that gets better every month, without us lifting a finger.
BHA is a new interface between mind and machine.
And this is just the first picture.
